comply-in.span: RAG queries are cheap per token retrieved; long context windows spike inference cost exponentially with input length. We'll calculate your actual cost per query.
Long context models often hallucinate on mid-document details; RAG with chunked retrieval maintains higher precision on specific facts. We measure both.
RAG can pull live data or updated indexes without retraining; long context windows are static snapshots. We'll show the freshness trade-off in your use case.
The winning 2026 pattern uses RAG for factual retrieval and long context for summarization of retrieved chunks. We only recommend this when it beats both pure approaches.

sec-head.h2: What is RAG? What are Long Context Windows?

p: RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) retrieves relevant document chunks before generating an answer, keeping cost low and data fresh. Long context windows let a model process entire documents—up to millions of tokens—in a single pass, but at higher cost and with accuracy risks on fine-grained details. The 2026 debate isn't about which is better, but when each (or a hybrid) wins on cost, accuracy, and freshness.

sec-head.h2: RAG vs Long Context Windows: A 2026 Showdown

td: Low-cost, precise retrieval from large or dynamic corpora
Single-pass processing of entire documents without indexing
Factual Q&A, real-time data, and cost-sensitive production systems
Document-level summarization, narrative analysis, and long-form reasoning
$0.10–$0.50+ per query (depending on input length and model)
High on specific facts, lower on cross-document synthesis
High on overall narrative, lower on mid-document precision and recall
Real-time updates via index refresh or live APIs
Static; requires costly retraining or re-prompting for new data
~1–5 seconds (for full context prefill and generation)

p: Neither pure RAG nor pure long context wins universally. The standard production pattern is RAG for retrieval-heavy tasks and long context for summarization of retrieved chunks—a hybrid that balances cost, accuracy, and freshness. The million-token model hype hasn't replaced retrieval; it's become a complementary tool in the retrieval stack.
